title: The King of Mind in the Sky-Ocean
summary: Deluded for so long, the poet understands through the true guru's teaching: his king of mind has perished and, tottering, entered the sky-ocean; he looks, the ten directions are empty, and with the mind gone there is no sin and merit. Given the mark by the vajrakula, he loses it in the waters of the sky, and Bhāde, having taken abhāga, says he has lost the king of mind. Munidatta reads the sky-ocean and the sky's waters as clear light, the mark as the means of the fourth joy given by the vajra guru, and abhāga as the share of non-arising.

flags.note: The edition's heading line has only the rāga. I add the poet from the attribution bhādepādānāṃ ('of Bhādepāda') written before the song and emended out of 1a, as the Tibetan heading also names him (b+ha dra'i zhabs kyi'o). Drop '· Bhadrapāda' if a heading should carry only what its own line has.

lines.gloss: this much · time · I · stayed (was) · in own delusion
lines.en: For so long a time I stayed in my own [delusion]{moha};

flags.note: svamohem̐, 'in my own delusion' (sva-moha). The Tibetan line has 'utterly deluded' (shin tu rmongs), as if reading su-, 'very', for sva-, 'own', or rendering freely; Munidatta cites only 'moham'. I follow the Bengali.

lines.gloss: now · by me (I) · understood · through the true guru's teaching (sadguru-bodha) · (refrain cue)
lines.en: now I have understood through the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching.

flags.note: boha (from bodha) can be 'awakening, understanding' or the guru's 'instruction'. With the Tibetan gsung, 'speech, word', I chose 'teaching'. Alternative: 'through the true guru's awakening'.

lines.gloss: now · king of mind (citta-rāja) · my (to me) · perished (naṣṭa)
lines.en: Now my [king of mind]{king-of-mind} has perished;

flags.note: ṇaṭhā (naṣṭa) covers 'destroyed, perished, lost, vanished'. I chose 'has perished', which suits a king and Munidatta's vinaṣṭa. The Tibetan line softens it to 'has been pacified' (zhi bar gyur). Alternatives: 'is destroyed', 'is lost', 'is gone'.

lines.gloss: in the sky-ocean (gaaṇa-samudda) · tottering · entered (praviṣṭa) · (refrain cue)

flags.note: ṭaliā: 'tottering, slipping, being shifted'. The Tibetan has 'by moving strongly' (rab tu bskyod pas). Alternative: 'slipping, it has gone into the sky-ocean'.
gaṇa- is read as gaaṇa, 'sky', with the glossary and the Tibetan (nam mkha'); as written it could be gaṇa, 'host, troop'.

lines.gloss: I see · ten directions · all · empty
lines.en: I look: in the [ten directions]{dasadis} all is [emptiness]{sunyata};

flags.note: śūna is the adjective 'empty'. The glossary's English for sunyata is the noun 'emptiness', which I used (the Tibetan line also has the noun, stong pa nyid). If 'empty' may stand as a variant, read 'all is empty'.

lines.translit: cia bihunne pāpa na punna || dhru ||
lines.gloss: mind · being deprived (vihīna) · sin · not · merit · (refrain cue)
lines.en: with the [mind]{citta} gone, there is no [sin and merit]{papa-punya}.

flags.note: bihunne (vihīna, locative): 'the mind being absent', hence 'with the mind gone'; 'without mind' is also possible. pāpa na punna is literally 'sin, not merit', that is, neither; rendered with the glossary phrase as 'no sin and merit'.

lines.gloss: by bājula (vajrakula) · gave · to me + mark (lakkhu?) · having told
lines.en: The [vajrakula]{vajrakula} spoke the [mark]{laksya} and gave it to me,

flags.note: bājule. Decision: I kept the glossary's source form and wrote 'the vajrakula', a designation rather than a personal name, following Munidatta, who renders the word vajrakulena, 'by the vajra family', and goes straight on with 'by the vajra guru'. The Tibetan line has a name, Rāhula (rA hu la), though its comment explains it as 'vajra family'. Alternatives: 'Vajrakula' as a name; the Old Bengali form 'Bājula'; or 'Rāhula' with the Tibetan line. Reviewer to decide.

mohakakhu is read as 'to me' + 'the mark' (lakkhu, lakṣya), with Munidatta (mahyaṃ ... lakṣyam) and the Tibetan (bdag la mtshan ma), not moha, 'delusion'. The written kakhu then stands for lakkhu, or its ka is a slip for la.
The Tibetan line names the giver Rāhula and has 'having told the mark, gave it' (mtshan ma smras nas byin); see the witness note on this line.

lines.gloss: by me (I) · lost (? or: ate) · in the sky · in the water (pāṇi?) · (refrain cue)
lines.en: I lost it in the waters of the [sky]{gagana}.

flags.note: ahārila: either 'lost' (compare Bengali hārā, 'to lose'; the Tibetan line has stor bar gyur, 'was lost') or 'ate, made a meal of' (from āhāra, 'food'). Munidatta repeats the word (ahārīkṛtam) without explaining it, and the Tibetan comment has 'made given' (ster bar byas). I chose 'lost'. With the other sense: 'I made a meal of it in the waters of the sky'.

paṇiām̐ is taken as pāṇi, 'water', as both Munidatta's 'ocean of clear light' and the Tibetan line's 'sky-ocean' imply. The glossary's sky-ocean entry treats the Bengali of 4b as having only 'in the sky'.
No object is expressed; 'it' is supplied. The Tibetan supplies 'my mind' (bdag gi sems); Munidatta's paraphrase points to what the guru gave, the mark.

abhāga is kept in source form, per the glossary, and construed as the object of laiā, 'having taken', with Munidatta and the Tibetan. Another construal makes it the poet's epithet, 'the luckless one' (Bengali abhāgā).
The Tibetan line has an imperative, 'take up the partless!' (cha shas med pa rab tu long), where the Bengali has the participle laiā, 'having taken'.
The poet names himself Bhāde; I kept that form and marked it with p-bhadra, whose English is Bhadrapāda.

lines.gloss: king of mind · by me (I) · ahāra (lost? food?) · made · (refrain cue)
lines.en: I have lost the [king of mind]{king-of-mind}.

flags.note: ahāra kaelā, 'made ahāra', rendered 'have lost', as in 4b. The Tibetan line has 'my king of mind itself was lost' (stor bar gyur); Munidatta paraphrases 'made to enter' the ocean. Alternative: 'I have made a meal of the king of mind'.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; the song is sung to the rāga Mallārī. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name (mal la ri) and calls it a melody (glu dbyangs).

The poet's name in the English heading comes from the attribution bhādepādānāṃ ('of Bhādepāda', that is Bhadrapāda) that the manuscript writes before the song; the edition's heading line has only the rāga, and the emendation removes the attribution from 1a. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names him in its heading: 'the melody called Mal la ri, of Bhadrapāda' (b+ha dra'i zhabs kyi'o).

Munidatta introduces the song: the siddha master [Bhadrapāda]{p-bhadra}, endowed with the delight of the joy of knowledge (jñānānandapramoda), sets out 'that very meaning' (cp.35.m1). He then takes the couplets in his usual order: the refrain makes the same meaning firm (cp.35.m3); his 'second verse' (couplet 3) states the nature of [practice]{abhyasa} (cp.35.m4); his 'third' (couplet 4) the power of the vajra (vajraprabhāva), where the Tibetan comment has 'the power of the vajra guru' (rdo rje bla ma'i mthu) (cp.35.m5); his 'fourth' (couplet 5) the poet's own nature (cp.35.m6).

eta kāla, 'this much time', is 'so long a time': kāla here is plain time, not the Kāla (Death) of song 1. hām̐u is 'I', acchilem̐ 'I was, I stayed', and svamohem̐ is sva-moha, 'one's own delusion', with the locative ending.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'though I stayed for that long, I was utterly deluded' (de tsam dus su 'dug kyang bdag ni shin tu rmongs). Its 'utterly' (shin tu), where the Bengali has sva-, 'own', may reflect a different reading (su-, 'very') or a free rendering. Munidatta cites only moham, 'delusion', which does not settle it (cp.35.m2).

Munidatta glosses 'so long a time' as 'in beginningless [saṃsāra]{samsara}' and adds 'through association with a [spiritual friend]{kalyanamitra}', a phrase whose link to the rest is unclear (the Tibetan comment has the same: dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang phrad pa). 'Delusion', he says, is attachment to outer [sense objects]{visaya}, through which he remained to the end of many aeons. 'Now, by the power of the Buddha, through the true guru's teaching, I have understood the [true nature]{svarupa} of mind.' The Tibetan comment has 'by meeting the true guru' and says the nature of his mind 'becomes suchness' (de kho na nyid du 'gyur) (cp.35.m2).

sadgurubohem̐: boha is from bodha, 'awakening, understanding', with the instrumental ending. Munidatta keeps the word (sadgurubodha) (cp.35.m2); the Tibetan line has 'from the speech of the true guru' (bla ma dam pa'i gsung las). I translate 'teaching'.
ciarāa is cittarāja, 'king of mind'; makum̐ is 'my, to me' (Munidatta: mama); ṇaṭhā is from naṣṭa, 'destroyed, perished, lost'. Munidatta has vinaṣṭa, 'destroyed' (cp.35.m3).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'now my king of mind has become pacified' (da ni bdag gi sems kyi rgyal po zhi bar gyur), a milder verb than ṇaṭhā. Its comment says the king of mind 'became nonexistent' (med par gyur) (cp.35.m3).

gaṇasamude: the glossary takes gaṇa as a contraction of gaaṇa, 'sky', hence 'in the sky-ocean' (locative -e), which the Tibetan nam mkha' rgya mtshor and Munidatta's gloss of 'sky' in 4b as an ocean support (cp.35.m5); read as written, gaṇa would be 'host, troop'. ṭaliā is 'tottering, slipping, being shifted' (compare Bengali ṭalā, 'to waver, be moved'); the Tibetan has 'by moving strongly' (rab tu bskyod pas). paiṭhā is from praviṣṭa, 'entered'; the Tibetan has 'arrived' (sleb par gyur).
The mind is pictured as a king who perishes and, tottering, goes into the sky, which is pictured as an ocean.

Munidatta says the refrain makes the same meaning firm: 'now, in the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the union of [vajra]{vajra} (pavi) and [lotus]{lotus}, my king of mind, its going destroyed (vinaṣṭagamana), has entered natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}' (cp.35.m3). His paraphrase puts natural clear light where the song has the sky-ocean, without an explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment agrees (rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal la rab tu zhugs). vinaṣṭagamana may mean that the king's movement is destroyed, or may gloss its destruction as a going.

pekhami is 'I see, I look' (from prekṣ-); dahadiha 'the ten directions' (daśa diśa); sarbbai 'all, everything'; śūna 'empty' (śūnya), an adjective. The Tibetan line has the noun stong pa nyid, 'emptiness'.

Munidatta says couplet 3 states the nature of [practice]{abhyasa}: 'by the yoga of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all dharmas, whatever quarter I look at appears all empty, made of [clear light]{prabhasvara}'. He goes on: 'therefore, through the non-arising of mind, I know sin, merit and the rest, and the bondage of saṃsāra', a compressed sentence without the song's negative. He supports it with a verse of [Saraha]{p-saraha}, cited by its opening words, aṅgem̐ pacchem̐, 'before, after' (cp.35.m4).

bihunne is from vihīna, 'lacking, deprived of', in the locative: 'the mind being absent'. The Tibetan has 'being parted from mind' (sems dang rnam par bral bas). pāpa na punna is literally 'sin, not merit', that is, neither sin nor merit.

The Tibetan comment differs from the Sanskrit (cp.35.m4). Where Munidatta has 'through the non-arising of mind' (cittasyānudayena), it has 'by the rising of the fourth' (bzhi pa shar bas), presumably the fourth joy, and it reads 'I know that sin, merit and the rest bind one in saṃsāra' ('khor bar 'ching bar bdag gis shes pa). It gives Saraha's verse as sngon dang phyi ma, 'before and after'.

vajrakula, 'vajra family': in the tantras, one of the families into which buddhas, deities and practitioners are grouped. The song has bājule, the instrumental of bājula, 'by bājula'; Munidatta renders it vajrakulena, 'by the vajra family' (cp.35.m5). The change vajrakula > bājula is regular in Middle Indic (compare rāula, 'king', from rājakula, 'royal house'), and that parallel shows how a 'family' word could come to name a person of rank. Whether bājula here is a title, a name, or the family itself is uncertain.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has a name: 'Rāhula, having told me the mark, gave it' (rA hu la yis bdag la mtshan ma smras nas byin). Its exemplar may have read rāhula (or rāula) here, or the translators took the word as a name. Yet the Tibetan comment cites rA hu la, explains it as 'to the vajra family' (rdo rje'i rigs la), and goes on 'by the vajra guru' (rdo rje bla mas), as the Sanskrit does (cp.35.m5).

mohakakhu: Munidatta's paraphrase has mahyaṃ, 'to me', and lakṣyam, 'the mark' (cp.35.m5), and the Tibetan line has bdag la mtshan ma, 'to me, the mark'. So moha- here is the first-person pronoun, 'to me', not moha, 'delusion', and kakhu apparently stands for lakkhu (lakṣya), unless the manuscript's ka is a slip for la. bhaṇiā is 'having told'; the Tibetan has smras nas, 'having spoken'.
Literally, someone (bājula) tells the poet a mark and hands it to him; the song does not say what the mark is.

Munidatta: by the vajra guru the 'mark', which he explains as what is to be meditated on, the means of the fourth [joy]{ananda}, was given to me; 'and I in turn, by devoted and uninterrupted [practice]{abhyasa}', made it ahāra 'in the ocean of [clear light]{prabhasvara}', which is how he glosses 'sky' (cp.35.m5). He repeats ahāra as ahārīkṛtam without explaining it.

In the Tibetan comment the vajra guru 'indicates' (mtshon nas) and then comes 'freed from things' (dngos po las grol nas): the translators divided Munidatta's bhāvyamuktaṃ as bhāva-muktaṃ, 'freed from entities', not bhāvyam uktaṃ, 'what is to be meditated on is meant'. At the end it has 'made it given into the ocean of clear light' ('od gsal gyi rgya mtshor ster bar byas), where its line has 'lost' (stor) (cp.35.m5).

ahārila is the past of a verb ahār-; 5b has the noun with 'made' (ahāra kaelā). Two senses seem possible: 'lost', as with Bengali hārā, 'to lose', which the Tibetan line supports (stor bar gyur, 'was lost'); or 'ate, made a meal of', from āhāra, 'food'. I translate 'lost'. gaaṇata is 'in the sky' (locative -ta); paṇiām̐ is apparently pāṇi, 'water', so 'in the sky's water', which Munidatta (prabhāsvarasamudre, 'in the ocean of clear light') and the Tibetan line (nam mkha'i rgya mtshor, 'into the sky-ocean') both read as an ocean (cp.35.m5). The line names no object: the Tibetan supplies 'my mind' (bdag gi sems), while in Munidatta's paraphrase it seems to be what the guru gave; my 'it' leaves the object open.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'in the sky-ocean my mind was lost' (nam mkha'i rgya mtshor bdag gi sems ni stor bar gyur): it gives the line a subject, mind, and the sky-ocean of the refrain.

abhāga is kept in source form because its sense is uncertain. Sanskrit abhāga is 'having no share', Bengali abhāgā 'unfortunate', and the Tibetan line has cha shas med pa, 'partless', reading a-bhāga as 'without parts'. I take it, with Munidatta (cp.35.m6) and the Tibetan, as the object of laiā, 'having taken'; it could also be the poet's epithet, 'the luckless one'. Bhāde is a short form of the poet's name, Bhadra(pāda).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'Bhadra said: take up the partless!' (b+ha dras smras pa cha shas med pa rab tu long), with an imperative (long, 'take!') where the Bengali has the participle laiā, 'having taken'. Its comment has the past, 'I have taken' (bdag gis blangs pa), and translates the poet's name as bzang po'i zhabs (cp.35.m6).

Munidatta says the last couplet states the poet's own nature (ātmasvarūpa), and glosses abhāga: 'I, Bhadrapāda, who have taken the share of [non-arising]{anutpada}' (anutpādabhāga). For 5b he says: the king of mind, the support of the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of beginningless existence, I have made enter the ocean of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all dharmas (cp.35.m6). The Tibetan comment agrees.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'my king of mind itself was lost' (bdag gi sems kyi rgyal po nyid ni stor bar gyur), intransitive, where the Bengali says 'I made the king of mind ahāra'. Munidatta paraphrases with 'made to enter' (praveśitaṃ) the ocean (cp.35.m6). On ahāra see the note on 4b.

termsOmitted.reason: eta kāla is 'so long a time': kāla is plain time here, not the Kāla (Death) of song 1.
মোহ in মোহকখু is 'to me' (Munidatta mahyaṃ, Tibetan bdag la), not delusion.
Tibetan-only hit: the Tibetan line supplies 'my mind' (bdag gi sems); the Bengali has no word for mind.
Tibetan-only hit: the Tibetan has 'sky-ocean' (nam mkha'i rgya mtsho); the Bengali has gaaṇata paṇiām̐, 'in the sky's water', rendered with sky (gagana) and 'waters'.
Tibetan-only hit: cha shas med pa, 'partless', is the Tibetan rendering of abhāga, which the glossary keeps in source form.

proposals.definition: A mark: what is pointed out or aimed at (Sanskrit lakṣya). In song 35 (4a) the poet is told the mark and given it; the written kakhu apparently stands for lakkhu. Munidatta explains the mark as what is to be meditated on (cp.35.m5). The Tibetan line has mtshan ma.
proposals.symbolicImage: the mark the poet is told and given (4a)

symbolicReadings.referent: what is to be meditated on (bhāvya), the means of the fourth joy (caturthānandopāya), which the vajra guru gave the poet; the Tibetan comment has the vajra guru 'indicate' (mtshon nas) it

forbiddenInLine: what is to be meditated on
proposals.rationale: 4a turns on the mark, on which Munidatta (lakṣya) and the Tibetan (mtshan ma) agree, and the glossary has no entry for it; lakṣya also underlies entries already in the glossary (alakṣya, durlakṣya). An entry links the word to 'mark' and keeps মোহকখু from being read as delusion.

questions: 4a bājule (flagged high): I wrote 'the vajrakula', using the glossary's source form as a designation, since Munidatta renders it vajrakulena and goes straight on with 'by the vajra guru'. Do you want a designation ('the vajrakula'), a name ('Vajrakula'), the Old Bengali form ('Bājula'), or the Tibetan line's Rāhula? Since the song never has the Sanskrit form, should the entry carry bājula as a variant?
4a mohakakhu: I read 'to me ... the mark' with Munidatta and the Tibetan and proposed a new entry, laksya ('mark'). Keep the proposal, or leave 'mark' unlinked?

4b and 5b ahār-: I chose 'lost' (the Tibetan lines' stor; compare Bengali hārā) over 'ate, made a meal of' (āhāra). The Tibetan comment's ster, 'give', and Munidatta's 'made to enter' leave it open. Which do you prefer?

4b paṇiām̐: I read 'in the waters of the sky' and linked sky (gagana), not sky-ocean. The sky-ocean entry says the Bengali of 4b has only 'in the sky'. Should that definition be revised, or should 4b link to sky-ocean?
2a ṇaṭhā: 'has perished', or 'is destroyed' / 'is lost'? The Tibetan line softens it to 'pacified'.
3a: may 'empty' be a variant of sunyata for the adjective śūna? I used 'emptiness', as the glossary requires.
5a: may 'Bhāde' be a variant of p-bhadra for the signature line? I kept the poet's own form.
h1: is it right to add '· Bhadrapāda' from the attribution written before the song, when the heading line itself has only the rāga?
